concept.name: Volume-open-interest analysis
concept.definition: A technical-analysis framework for futures markets that interprets price trends jointly with trading volume and open interest to judge whether a move is supported by new positioning or by liquidation of existing positions. It is an analytical framework or heuristic, not a proven predictive law.
concept.intuition: Price tells you where the market went; volume tells you how much business was done; open interest tells you whether traders are staying or leaving — read together, they describe the 'conviction' behind a move.
concept.mechanics: The classic readings: price up + volume up + OI up is taken as a strong trend (new money entering); price up + OI down suggests short covering (weaker); price down + OI up suggests new shorts entering; price down + OI down suggests long liquidation. The CFTC glossary notes chartists plot trends of price movements, volume of trading, and open interest together.
concept.failure_modes: The framework is unfalsifiable in its loose form — the same OI/volume pattern can be rationalized as bullish or bearish after the fact. Roll periods, spread trading, and block/EFP activity distort both volume and OI, and rising electronic market-making has weakened the link between OI changes and directional conviction.
concept.misconceptions: High volume does not 'confirm' a trend in any causal sense, and OI cannot show net bullishness because every contract has a long and a short. The rules of thumb come from practitioner lore, not from validated statistical models.
concept.example: Wheat rallies 3% on record volume while total open interest climbs 8%: the analyst reads new longs and shorts entering and treats the breakout as position-backed; a similar rally on falling OI would be read as short covering and viewed with more suspicion.

citations.source: CFTC Futures Glossary: A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry
